title: From Universal Consciousness to the Individual
reflection: Once today, when a strong feeling arrives, say: this is here, and I am the one noticing it. What opens up?

questions.q: How does one boundless awareness come to appear as you, according to Conversation 2.1?
o: Through three linked movements happening now: localisation, limitation and identification.
By creating a second reality, in which each person is made as a separate and new being.
By a single event long ago, which fixed each person as one separate individual for good.
By the brain alone, which makes awareness out of matter when it reaches some complexity.
questions.e: The question of Module 2 is answered without a second reality. Localisation centres awareness in one body-mind; limitation contracts what is known and attended to; identification takes that viewpoint as the whole of who you are. The result is the jīva.

questions.q: What is limitation, saṅkoca, in Conversation 2.1?
o: The boundless now working through a finite channel: awareness is contracted in expression only.
The shrinking of awareness itself, which really does become smaller in each separate person.
The loss of memory with age, as the body and the brain wear out over a lifetime.
The rule that a person must keep to their own place, and so never meet the world fully.
questions.e: The awareness is not made smaller in itself, only contracted in expression: you know, attend to and remember only a little. The window framing sunlight into a beam is the image.

questions.q: A woman feels that nothing is lacking in a seed, yet it is tiny. What does Conversation 2.1 take from the great tree in the seed?
o: Nothing is missing in you; the whole is only condensed, in contracted form.
The tree is gone from the seed, and the person must grow it back by hard work.
The tree is a different thing, which is added to the seed from the outside later on.
The seed is the whole of a person, so there is no tree for her to find in herself.
questions.e: The Pratyabhijñā Hṛdayam says the individual, though contracted, is of the nature of the whole universe in contracted form. Nothing is missing; it is just condensed.
questions.c: Nothing is missing in you; it is condensed

questions.q: A man says, “I am anxious,” and feels filled by it. What does Conversation 2.1 suggest?
o: Widen the frame: anxiety is here, and I am the one noticing it, which opens a gap.
Say I am not anxious, so that the feeling is pushed away and no longer takes hold.
Treat the feeling as the whole of himself, since it is the thing that he feels most.
Wait for the feeling to end, and only then ask what it was that he had been feeling.
questions.e: I am anxious collapses the sky into one storm. The widening move opens a gap between the feeling and the one who has it. Modern therapy calls it defusion; the contemplative traditions have practised it for millennia.
questions.c: Anxiety is here, and I am the one noticing it

questions.q: “The true Self is the shifting, constructed I that changes from room to room.”
questions.e: That describes the sense of self, the weather. The true Self is the constant fact of being aware, the sky. The weather is real, but it is not the sky, and mistaking one for the other is avidyā.
questions.c: The shifting I is the weather; the true Self is the sky

questions.q: A student asks whether the science of the self and the contemplative traditions compete. How does Conversation 2.1 answer?
o: They answer different questions: science the formation of the self, the traditions its ground.
They answer one question, and one of them is simply right while the other is wrong.
They answer nothing alike, so a person must choose one and give the other up.
They answer the same question in different words, so nothing is gained by both.
questions.e: Science explains how the self is built: bodily boundary, viewpoint, memory, self-model, narrative and agency. The traditions describe what awareness itself is. They are companions and not rivals.
questions.c: Formation and ground are companions, not rivals

questions.q: “Individuality is just an illusion, so nothing in a person’s life really matters.”
questions.e: This is one of the two ditches the lesson warns of. Individuality is real as experience, necessary, and biologically and socially supported, though not the final truth of you. The balanced view is one awareness appearing through many real centres.
questions.c: Individuality is real as experience, not the final truth

questions.q: What does one sun reflected in many pots of water show, in Conversation 2.1?
o: Many reflections, genuinely different, from one undivided source: so compassion is accurate.
Many suns, each in its own pot, which have nothing at all to do with one another.
One pot only, since the other pots are not real and so cannot reflect anything.
One sun, which is dimmed by the pots and made a little less bright in each of them.
questions.e: One Consciousness-Energy, many body-minds. Unlike a passive pot, a living body-mind is an active expression of the same power. Genuine compassion is accurate and not just virtuous: the other is another reflection of the same sun.
questions.c: One sun, many pots: compassion is accurate

questions.q: A man keeps his distance from everyone, sure that each person is utterly sealed off. Which ditch is this, in Conversation 2.1?
o: Everyone-is-an-island, which makes compassion a mystery instead of a natural thing.
Nothing-really-matters, which uses the idea of illusion to withdraw from life.
The balanced view, since he sees clearly that each person is a separate centre.
The true Self, since he rests in the plain fact of being aware without any other.
questions.e: Everyone-is-an-island makes compassion a mystery. The other ditch, nothing-really-matters, dismisses individuality as illusion and can be misused to disengage from life.
questions.c: Everyone-is-an-island is one of the two ditches

questions.q: A teacher wants to notice the I being built in her day. Which step fits Conversation 2.1?
o: Catch one moment of identification, and say: this is the viewpoint, and I am aware of it.
Try to switch the viewpoint off, since it is the root of every problem she has.
Ignore the viewpoint, since it is only weather and has no bearing on how she lives.
Take the viewpoint as the whole of her, since she cannot know anything outside of it.
questions.e: The practical situation is to catch the I being built. Identification is the third movement, taking the localised, limited viewpoint as the whole. Seeing it as a viewpoint begins to loosen it.
questions.c: Catch the I being built, and see it as a viewpoint
